projects.title: OpenFOAM Thermal Verification
projects.summary: An automated workflow that checks OpenFOAM heat-transfer simulations against analytical solutions and energy balances.
projects.outcome: On the same coarse room model, continuing the run with a stricter stopping rule cut the wall energy imbalance from 7.96% to 0.918%.

media.alt: OpenFOAM results for heat radiated by a slab, heat leaving and stored in a cylinder, and the room’s wall energy balance
media.caption: The public benchmark checks heat radiated by a slab, heat leaving and stored in a cylinder, and the wall energy balance in a room model.
media.license: Project-authored public figure. See upstream OpenFOAM attribution in THIRD_PARTY.md.

sections.title: Why check the energy balance?
sections.text: The workflow checks the mesh and records how the solver converges. It then compares temperatures and heat flows with independent calculations. In the room radiation model, the solver met its stopping criteria while the wall energy imbalance was still above the study’s 5% tolerance.

sections.title: What changed in the second run
sections.text: The room run resumed from its previous endpoint on the same mesh, with the same number of radiation directions. It used a stricter convergence threshold for enthalpy and allowed more iterations. The wall energy imbalance then fell below 5%. In a separate set of slab benchmarks, all 21 configurations passed their checks.

sections.title: Scope of the benchmark
sections.text: These are numerical checks on the cases studied. Experimental validation and estimates of how the room result varies with mesh size or radiation directions remain open. The workflow shows why it helps to check the heat balance as well as the solver’s stopping criteria.

feature_media.alt: Wall heat flows and their net total as the OpenFOAM room run continues
feature_media.caption: Heat flow at the room walls and the net balance over the continued simulation.
feature_media.license: Project-authored public figure. See upstream OpenFOAM attribution in THIRD_PARTY.md.

featured_copy.problem: This workflow checks whether an OpenFOAM result balances the heat going in and out.
featured_copy.proof: The room model initially missed the 5% tolerance at 7.96%. A stricter stopping rule brought the imbalance down to 0.918%.

projects.title: Evidence-Based Scientific Writing Editor
projects.summary: A set of instructions for Codex that helps authors plan, draft and revise papers around the results they can support.
projects.outcome: The Editor checks whether each claim follows from the results and helps plan the order of figures and arguments.

sections.title: Review a draft or plan a paper
sections.text: The Editor reads the results and manuscript before suggesting changes. It can help decide what a paper should claim, where each figure belongs and what to revise in a draft. Its public guide lists 14 rules and states the confidence behind each one.

sections.title: Keep the author in charge of the claim
sections.text: Two rules ask Codex to state what the study observed before suggesting why it happened, and to keep uncertainty visible when a mechanism has yet to be shown. The author decides whether to accept changes in meaning. The public files show how the skill works. Its effect on manuscript quality has yet to be measured.

projects.title: Distill Scientific Writing Method
projects.summary: A set of instructions for Codex that turns a selected group of papers into a writing guide, with examples and exceptions for each rule.
projects.outcome: Python scripts set up the review files and check that each draft rule includes its sources.

sections.title: Find patterns across papers
sections.text: The skill helps an analyst compare how authors explain methods, present results and qualify claims. It records what the papers show, what an author says about their choices and what the analyst infers. When examples disagree or the author’s contribution is unclear, the notes record that uncertainty.

sections.title: Turn the notes into a writing guide
sections.text: The skill writes a guide and a table linking each rule to examples and exceptions. A reviewer decides which rules are well supported and where they apply. The companion Editor can use a reviewed guide when working on another manuscript.

sections.title: Check the files before using the guide
sections.text: In a check of the public scripts, the setup script created the expected files and refused to overwrite a populated directory. The checker caught incomplete records. The reviewer still decides whether the examples support the proposed rules.

projects.title: Top-Journal Palette Miner
projects.summary: A browser tool that analyses colours in scientific figures and suggests how to use them in a new chart.
projects.outcome: Inspect a figure and check colour contrast in your browser. Export palette choices as JSON or CSS and save a report from Transfer Lab.

media.alt: Palette Lab Inspect interface showing extracted colour candidates and visual roles for its built-in synthetic figure
media.caption: The Inspect tab shows colour swatches and possible roles for a built-in example.
media.license: Capture of the owner’s public MIT-licensed interface and original synthetic example.

sections.title: Inspect colours in a figure
sections.text: Inspect samples colours from an image in your browser. It shows how common each colour is, suggests roles such as a data series, a neutral or a highlight, and checks contrast against white. Check those suggestions against what the figure is meant to communicate.

sections.title: Try the palette on a new figure
sections.text: Transfer uses the new figure’s chart type, number of series and planned emphasis to suggest which colours to use. It flags cases where the recommendation is uncertain. The built-in example warns when it cannot find a clear neutral. Check that the result is readable and the emphasis still makes sense before using the export.

sections.title: Where the examples come from
sections.text: The images on this page are original synthetic examples. The repository also includes separately licensed examples and lists their sources and any changes.

gallery.alt: Three original synthetic figure examples showing paired series, an ordered response and rare emphasis colours
gallery.caption: Three synthetic examples showing different jobs for colour in a figure.
gallery.license: Original project artwork under MIT. Third-party figures are not redistributed here.

featured_copy.problem: See which colours in a figure carry the data, provide context or draw the reader’s eye.
featured_copy.proof: Transfer Lab suggests colours for a new figure. Review the choices and export them as JSON, CSS or a report.

projects.title: Career Intelligence Lab
projects.summary: A bilingual tool for researchers and engineers to track job opportunities, match their experience to requirements and draft applications.
projects.outcome: The public demo shows where a match comes from and which points need checking. The local workspace supports drafting in English and Simplified Chinese.

sections.title: Match experience to the role
sections.text: The tool distinguishes direct and transferable matches from possible matches that need a check, as well as gaps and missing information. It keeps the same source references in English and Simplified Chinese. New or edited translations stay out of the draft until reviewed. You can still see which original sources support a match.

sections.title: Work with your own records locally
sections.text: The single-user workspace and command-line tool use the same local JSON file. The software checks the file version before saving and writes updates as a single operation. The public demo uses fictional candidate data. The applicant checks the matches, sources and wording before using a draft.

sections.title: What was tested
sections.text: All 14 automated tests using fictional data passed in the repository review. A separate Chromium walkthrough covered saving, translation review and draft checks. Tests cover the workflow. Hiring outcomes and multi-user use have yet to be studied.

media.alt: Career Intelligence Lab demo showing a job requirement, a possible match, its source and a question to check
media.caption: The public demo uses fictional candidate information. Here, it shows a possible match and a question the candidate needs to check.
media.license: Portfolio capture of the owner’s MIT-licensed public demo, using its synthetic fixture.

featured_copy.problem: Find out which parts of your experience match a role and where you need more information.
featured_copy.proof: The demo shows the source behind a match. Translated wording stays out of a draft until it has been checked.

projects.title: Personal Investment Research
projects.summary: A Python research tool for comparing investment plans under the same assumptions, developed after a trading rule performed poorly on historical data.
projects.outcome: The offline tool screens a catalogue against user constraints. The plan comparison keeps a record of cash and holdings.

media.alt: Offline comparison of four investment plans using simulated pound prices, with a drawdown check
media.caption: The recorded demo compares four plans using the same simulated prices, deposits and costs.
media.license: Project-authored media under the project’s MIT licence.

sections.title: What the historical test showed
sections.text: I set out to test a rule for buying stocks after a price drop. The historical simulation made a profit in 2 of 14 complete quarters outside the training period. It lagged a buy-and-hold comparison with matched capital in all 14. The result depends on which stocks were included and how orders were simulated. Data vendors may revise records, some data had been inspected before the test, and daily prices do not show which price was reached first.

sections.title: Compare plans under the same conditions
sections.text: The offline tool screens a catalogue against the user’s constraints and can return an empty list. Its example compares a 60/40 allocation with holding cash, buying and holding a broad equity investment, and investing in stages. All four use the same simulated pound prices, deposits and costs. The example checks the workflow. Its usefulness in real markets remains untested.

sections.title: How I worked with AI on the project
sections.text: I set the research question, chose the comparison baselines and kept the poor historical result in the record. ChatGPT and Codex helped with source research, protocol design, implementation and testing. The output is for comparing assumptions in a research setting. It gives no investment recommendation or trade instruction.
